passages.t: A sealed scroll, and no one worthy
passages.happening:
John is still looking at the throne room of chapter 4. Now he sees something in God's hand: “Then I saw a scroll in the right hand of the One seated on the throne. It had writing on both sides and was sealed with seven seals” (verse 1).

He hears a mighty angel call out with a loud voice: “Who is worthy to break the seals and open the scroll?” (verse 2). No one answers. “But no one in heaven or on earth or under the earth was able to open the scroll or look inside it” (verse 3).

And John weeps: “And I began to weep bitterly, because no one was found worthy to open the scroll or look inside it” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
A scroll was the ancient form of a book: a long sheet rolled up. This one is written on both sides, so it is full, and it is closed with seven seals, so it is fully shut. The Greek word for it, biblion, could mean a book, a legal deed or a will. Only someone with the right authority could break its seals.

The scroll holds God's purposes for the world, his judgment and his redemption. While it stays shut, those purposes are not carried out. That is why the angel's question matters, and why the silence that follows is so heavy. Heaven, earth and the world of the dead are searched, and no one is worthy.

So John weeps. He does not weep politely. He weeps ‘bitterly’. The churches he writes to were small and under pressure. They needed to know that God's purposes would not stay sealed for ever, that someone could open history and carry it to its end. For a moment it seems that no one can.

His tears are not rebuked as a lack of faith. They are answered.
passages.ot:
Ezekiel too was shown a full scroll: “Then I looked and saw a hand reaching out to me, and in it was a scroll, which He unrolled before me. And written on the front and back of it were words of lamentation, mourning, and woe” (Ezekiel 2:9-10).

And Daniel was told to close up his visions: “But you, Daniel, shut up these words and seal the book until the time of the end” (Daniel 12:4). In Revelation the sealed book of God's purposes is about to be opened.
passages.hard:
What is the scroll?

Readers take it in a few ways, and they often overlap. Roman wills were commonly sealed by seven witnesses and opened only at the proper time by the proper person, and some interpreters think John's first hearers would have heard the scroll as a testament whose inheritance only the rightful heir could release. Others see the sealed book of Daniel 12:4, closed until the time of the end. Others see Ezekiel's scroll, written on front and back. These notes do not choose.

On every reading the point is the same. The scroll holds what God means to do in the world, to judge evil and to save his people, and the question of the chapter is who has the right to open it.
passages.asks: Ask whether you have ever wept, as John did, because it seemed that no one could put the world right. Ask what you do with that grief. And ask whether you believe that God's purposes for the world are written and will be opened.

passages.t: The Lion who is a Lamb
passages.happening:
One of the elders speaks to John: “Do not weep! Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has triumphed to open the scroll and its seven seals” (verse 5).

John hears of a lion. Then he turns and sees something else: “Then I saw a Lamb who appeared to have been slain, standing in the center of the throne, encircled by the four living creatures and the elders. The Lamb had seven horns and seven eyes, which represent the seven Spirits of God sent out into all the earth” (verse 6).

“And He came and took the scroll from the right hand of the One seated on the throne” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
This is the hinge of the whole book.

The elder's titles are Israel's great hopes. ‘The Lion of the tribe of Judah’ goes back to Jacob's blessing on Judah, the tribe of the kings. ‘The Root of David’ goes back to Isaiah's promise of a king from David's family on whom the Spirit would rest. Many in John's day hoped for a conquering king who would break the power of their enemies.

John hears of a lion. He turns and sees a Lamb. Revelation often works this way: John hears one thing, then sees another, and what he sees explains what he heard. The Lion has won, but he won by being slain. The conquering king conquers by dying.

The Greek word for lamb here, arnion, is a small, even tender word. It is Revelation's main name for Christ, used of him twenty-eight times in the book. The Lamb ‘appeared to have been slain’, or more literally stands ‘as slain’. He is alive, standing, yet he still bears the marks of his death. The resurrection did not erase the cross. The risen Christ reigns as the Lamb who was killed.

Yet he is not weak. Horns in the Bible are a picture of strength, and seven horns picture complete power. The seven eyes are the seven Spirits of God, sent out into all the earth: the Lamb sees everything, and his Spirit goes everywhere.

And he stands ‘in the center of the throne’. He is not beside the throne as a servant. He shares it. He takes the scroll from God's own hand, and from this moment every seal that is broken, every judgment and every rescue in the chapters that follow comes from his hand.
passages.ot:
The Lion is from Jacob's blessing: “Judah is a young lion” and “The scepter will not depart from Judah, nor the staff from between his feet” (Genesis 49:9-10).

The Root is Isaiah's: “Then a shoot will spring up from the stump of Jesse, and a Branch from his roots will bear fruit” (Isaiah 11:1), and “On that day the Root of Jesse will stand as a banner for the peoples” (Isaiah 11:10).

The Lamb recalls the Passover, when the blood of a lamb on the doorposts of Israel's houses kept them safe: “when I see the blood, I will pass over you” (Exodus 12:13). It recalls too the servant in Isaiah who suffered for others: “He was led like a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is silent, so He did not open His mouth” (Isaiah 53:7).

The seven eyes come from Zechariah: “these seven eyes of the LORD, which scan the whole earth” (Zechariah 4:10).
passages.asks: Ask where you expect God to act with force, when he may be working through faithfulness and suffering instead. Ask what it means that Christ still bears the marks of his death. And ask how it changes the way you think about power, in your home, your work or your church, that the one on the throne is a Lamb who was slain.

passages.happening:
When the Lamb takes the scroll, John sees the living creatures and the elders fall down before him: “Each one had a harp, and they were holding golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints” (verse 8).

And he hears them sing: “And they sang a new song: ‘Worthy are You to take the scroll and open its seals, because You were slain, and by Your blood You purchased for God those from every tribe and tongue and people and nation. You have made them to be a kingdom and priests to serve our God, and they will reign upon the earth’” (verses 9-10).
passages.hearers:
In chapter 4 the elders fell down before the One on the throne. Now they fall down before the Lamb. The same worship is given to both.

They hold harps and golden bowls of incense. Both belong to the worship of the temple. And the book tells us what the incense is: ‘the prayers of the saints’. In the New Testament ‘saints’ means all God's holy people, not a special class of Christians. The prayers of ordinary believers, in small and frightened churches, are not lost. They are kept in gold before the throne. In chapter 8 they will rise again.

Then they sing ‘a new song’. In the Psalms and in Isaiah a new song is the praise that answers a fresh act of God's rescue. Here the rescue is the cross.

The song gives its reason: ‘because You were slain, and by Your blood You purchased for God’. The word for purchased, agorazō, is a word of the marketplace. It pictures someone being bought out of one household into another, as a slave could be in that world. People now belong to God because the Lamb paid for them with his own blood.

And they come ‘from every tribe and tongue and people and nation’. The people of God was always meant to be drawn from every people on earth. No language, no race and no nation owns the Lamb.

Last, the Lamb has made them ‘a kingdom and priests’. That was God's calling to Israel at Sinai. Now it is given to people from every nation, to serve God and to reign with him.
passages.ot:
Prayer rising like incense is the psalm's picture: “May my prayer be set before You like incense, my uplifted hands like the evening offering” (Psalm 141:2).

The new song is the psalm's and the prophet's: “Sing to the LORD a new song; sing to the LORD, all the earth” (Psalm 96:1), and “Sing to the LORD a new song— His praise from the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 42:10).

And ‘a kingdom and priests’ is God's word to Israel at Sinai: “And unto Me you shall be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Exodus 19:6).
passages.asks: Ask what it means to you that your prayers are kept before God's throne, even the ones that seem unanswered. Ask whether your own church looks like a people drawn from ‘every tribe and tongue and people and nation’, and what would change if it did. And ask what it means to belong to God because you were bought at such a price.

passages.happening:
The circle of worship grows. John looks and hears “the voices of many angels and living creatures and elders encircling the throne, and their number was myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands” (verse 11). They cry out with a loud voice: “Worthy is the Lamb, who was slain, to receive power and riches and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and blessing!” (verse 12).

Then the circle grows wider still: “And I heard every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea, and all that is in them, saying: ‘To Him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be praise and honor and glory and power forever and ever!’” (verse 13).

“And the four living creatures said, ‘Amen,’ and the elders fell down and worshiped” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
The chapter builds in widening circles. First the living creatures and the elders. Then angels beyond counting: ‘myriads of myriads’, a myriad being ten thousand. Then every creature in heaven, on earth, under the earth and in the sea. And then the whole song is closed with one word, ‘Amen’.

The songs grow too. The first had a reason attached: ‘because You were slain’. The angels' song gives the Lamb seven things: power, riches, wisdom, strength, honour, glory and blessing. Seven is the number of completeness. Nothing is held back.

The first hearers lived in cities full of imperial ceremony. Emperors were greeted with acclamations when they entered a city. Their images were honoured with hymns and incense. Suetonius and Tacitus both report that Nero kept a trained group of young men to lead the applause when he performed. Scholars have long noticed that the songs of Revelation 4 and 5 sound like such acclamations, and that they turn them around. The one truly worthy of power and riches and glory is not the emperor. It is the Lamb, who was killed by imperial power.

And the last song is sung to two together: ‘To Him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb’. In chapter 4, the throne room praised God the Creator. Now the whole creation praises God and the Lamb in one breath. That is one of the highest moments in the New Testament's teaching about who Jesus is.
passages.ot:
The countless angels are Daniel's: “Thousands upon thousands attended Him, and myriads upon myriads stood before Him” (Daniel 7:10).

And the whole creation praising God is the psalms' hope. The last psalm ends: “Let everything that has breath praise the LORD” (Psalm 150:6).
passages.hard:
If only God may be worshipped, how can the Lamb be worshipped alongside him without making two gods?

The question is a fair one, and Revelation raises it itself. In the first century, Jewish faith prayed to one God and refused worship to any creature. Revelation shares that conviction completely. Twice John falls at the feet of an angel, and twice he is told, “Do not do that!” and “Worship God!” (19:10; 22:8-9). A thoughtful reader might suspect the book of contradicting itself, or of quietly adding a second god.

The church's answer, worked out over the first four centuries and confessed in the Nicene Creed (AD 325, expanded in 381), is that the worship of the Lamb is not the worship of a second being beside God. It is the worship of the one God, who is Father, Son and Spirit. Scholars of early Christianity have noted how quickly this kind of devotion to Jesus appeared among Jewish believers, well before the creeds gave it careful language. Revelation 5 does not explain the Trinity. But it shows the worship that the doctrine of the Trinity was worked out to account for. The Lamb shares the throne and the praise of the one God, and God does not stop being one.
passages.asks: Ask what it would mean for you to join a song that the whole creation is singing. Ask what you would add to the angels' list of what the Lamb is worthy to receive, and what you have held back from him. And ask whether you can say ‘Amen’ to this chapter with your life, not only with your lips.
